title: Active Scanning: Wordlist Scanning
summary: Wordlist scanning tries thousands of guessed names against a service to discover content and infrastructure that was never advertised. It is mechanically similar to credential brute force, but the objective is discovery rather than login: hidden directories, backup archives, administrative portals, application programming interface endpoints and cloud storage buckets whose globally unique names can simply be guessed. Wordlists range from generic lists of common file and folder names to target specific lists assembled from earlier reconnaissance, such as product names taken from job adverts or staff naming conventions. The signal is volume and shape rather than any single request, since each request is an ordinary looking web call and most generate a not found response. Web access logs, content delivery logs, bucket access logs and web application firewall counters are where the pattern shows, typically as many distinct paths from one source in a short window with a very high error rate. Defenders separate this from crawlers, monitoring and fuzzing in test environments by source reputation, path randomness and whether the words match anything the application legitimately serves.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker tries many guessed names against your website or cloud storage. They hope to find hidden pages, backup files or admin areas. It is like reading out names from a long list until one answers.
beginner.whyItMatters: Old and hidden pages often have weaker security than the main site. A guessed name can reveal an admin login or a copy of your data. Because the requests look normal one by one, the attack hides well. Only the pattern across many requests gives it away.
howItWorks: The attacker builds a list of likely names, such as admin, backup, test and common file endings.
They may improve the list with words taken from your website and job adverts.
Their tool requests each name from your web server, one after another, very quickly.
Most requests fail with a not found message, but a few return real pages or files.
They also guess cloud storage bucket names, because those names must be unique worldwide.
Anything found is examined for useful data, weak login pages or a later attack route.
beginner.example: Think of someone at a hotel reception trying every room number on a keypad, one after another. Each try is a normal action and no lock is broken. The moment one door clicks open, they know exactly which room has something worth taking.
takeaways: A burst of not found responses from one source is the main sign of wordlist scanning.
Delete backup files and unused admin pages instead of relying on nobody finding them.
Check cloud storage names and permissions, because bucket names are easy to guess.

objectives: Define wordlist scanning and explain how it differs from credential brute force.
Describe how generic and target specific wordlists are built.
Identify the log sources that reveal enumeration of web paths and buckets.
Explain why high error rates and path randomness indicate hostile enumeration.
Recommend content hygiene steps that remove discoverable leftovers.
